Q: Should we handle all things via plugins and components in october cms? A:

You can override the blog plugins components default markup with your own and add your author information there.

To do that you should learn about overriding plugin components markup here

https://octobercms.com/docs/cms/components#customizing-default-markup

I also think you would benefit by watching this video to help you understand how to use and set up Rainlab's blog plugin.

https://vimeo.com/97088926

Lastly, I dont think you need to use the onEnd() php function. The author/user information is available to you in {{ post }} and can accessed as you mentioned using... 

{{ post.user.first_name }}

Q: Multiple Tables or Single Table in PostgreSQL A:

What if the edit is merging more than one picture together? E.g., create a collage, add objects from multiple pictures into a scene from another? I'd say the result should have multiple parent links.

I'd vote for a single table with pictures, then another one for many-to-many links:
demo at db<>fiddle

create table images(
   id bigint generated always as identity primary key
 , url text
 , name text
 , client_id bigint references client(id)
 , product_id bigint references product(id)
 , created_at timestamptz );
create table image_edits(
   parent_id bigint references images(id)
 , child_id bigint references images(id) );

You could use inheritance to add fields related to specific types of edits

create table image_crops(
   corner1 point
 , corner2 point )
 inherits(image_edits);
create table image_rescales(
   percentage real)
 inherits(image_edits);

If you expect this hierarchy to grow large and complicated, you could consider adding Apache AGE to your Postgres. Once Postgres version 19 goes out of beta, you'll be also able to use native PGQ, which is based on the same Neo4J Cypher query language.

Q: How to get the number of rows from multiple related tables with one query A:

Consider (after allowing for "subset of ID's from 'A'" and "filtered by a range of timestamps"):

SELECT A.id,
    ( SELECT COUNT(*) FROM B WHERE B.id = A.ID WHERE ???) AS B_count,
    ( SELECT COUNT(*) FROM C WHERE C.id = A.ID WHERE ???) AS C_count,
    ( SELECT COUNT(*) FROM D WHERE D.id = A.ID WHERE ???) AS D_count
    FROM A
    WHERE ???

Q: Setting the statement name in PDO Prepared Statements A:

Caching prepared SQL statements (PREPARE name FROM ...) generally doesn’t make sense.

Prepared statements are session-local

Each connection has its own prepared statement namespace: a PREPARE name exists only for the current session. You cannot share prepared statements across connections.

Attempting to “cache prepared statements globally” is tricky. You would need to query performance_schema.prepared_statements_instances to see if the statement exists and belongs to your thread, i.e., match OWNER_THREAD_ID to your connection’s THREAD_ID via performance_schema.threads.

Even then, the performance_schema information is limited: it does not reveal metadata locks, pending result sets, or previous errors. You also cannot be sure the statement is still valid (e.g., if the underlying table has been dropped or altered).

Executing a prepared statement still requires extra setup

Each execution may require setting and binding variables, depending on the query.

These extra network round trips can partially offset the benefits of “preparing once.”

The performance benefit is usually small

MySQL/MariaDB still perform checks on table metadata, permissions, etc., on every execution.

In simple benchmarks, the difference between PREPARE once + EXECUTE and EXECUTE IMMEDIATE is typically very small (~4%).

Considering the added complexity of caching and checking performance_schema, such a solution will be actually slower and less stable.

Suggestion: Do not use PREPARE FROM sql statements for caching purposes. Instead, use prepared statements via the binary protocol, and close them as soon as they are no longer needed.

Q: Error in MariaDB query - difference to MySQL A:

As the MariaDB documentation for LAG() mentions, on MariaDB there is only a one or two (but not three) parameter version of the LAG() function:

LAG (expr[, offset]) OVER ( [ PARTITION BY partition_expression ] < ORDER BY order_list > )

The third parameter in MySQL corresponds to a default value, which kicks in when LAG() cannot find any previous record.

In this case, assuming that the electricity would never be null, we could use COALESCE() here to capture and replace the first call to LAG():

CASE season WHEN '2008/09' THEN 4029 
            WHEN '2013/14' THEN 3389 
            WHEN '2016/17' THEN 6367 
            WHEN '2018/19' THEN 5311
            ELSE electricity -
                 COALESCE(LAG(electricity, 1)
                          OVER (ORDER BY season), 106740) END AS consumed
